These findings define a STAT3-GPX4/SLC40A1-dependent mechanism underlying the anti-CRC activity of FLLL32 and support further investigation of STAT3-associated ferroptosis regulation as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in CRC.

title: Autism: epidemiology, genetics, molecular mechanisms, clinical features, diagnosis, and management
abstract: Abstract Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent deficits in social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviors. Global prevalence has risen steadily, yet reported rates vary markedly across regions and populations. These discrepancies reflect inequities in diagnostic access and screening capacity rather than true differences in incidence. This review integrates recent advances across the full ASD research spectrum. We first examine global epidemiological patterns and demographic disparities. We then dissect the genetic architecture of ASD, including rare and common variants, copy number variations, and gene–environment interactions that disrupt prenatal and early postnatal brain development. At the molecular level, diverse risk factors converge on shared neurodevelopmental mechanisms. These include synaptic dysfunction, dysregulated signaling through mTOR, Ras-ERK-MAPK, Wnt and Notch pathways, impaired neurogenesis, chronic neuroimmune inflammation, and excitatory–inhibitory imbalance. We also discuss how these mechanisms manifest in core clinical features, including social deficits, repetitive behaviors, and sensory abnormalities. We summarize current diagnostic standards and their limitations. Cross-species animal models, from Drosophila to non-human primates, are evaluated for their essential roles in mechanistic validation and therapeutic screening. Finally, we assess clinical management strategies, ranging from behavioral and educational interventions to pharmacological and supportive services. By tracing a continuous path from risk factors at the population level through molecular pathophysiology to interventions guided by mechanism, this review offers an integrative synthesis that connects basic discovery to clinical translation. We further discuss how multi-omics and artificial intelligence may advance precise diagnosis rooted in mechanism and personalized treatment.

title: Lysine-specific demethylase 1 (LSD1) regulates macrophage plasticity and immune checkpoint expression in colorectal liver metastases
abstract: Abstract Colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) are a major cause of mortality in colorectal cancer and are characterised by a profoundly immunosuppressive tumour microenvironment in which tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs) play a central role. However, the molecular mechanisms driving TAM plasticity and maintenance remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated macrophage heterogeneity in CRLM and examined the contribution of the epigenetic regulator lysine-specific demethylase 1 (LSD1) to TAM polarisation. Analysis of patient-derived specimens by flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry and transcriptional profiling identified a population of large TAMs (L-TAMs) enriched in the peritumoral niche that displayed an immunosuppressive, M2-like phenotype and was associated with poor clinical outcome. In contrast, smaller TAMs (S-TAMs) exhibited a more inflammatory transcriptional programme, including increased IL1β expression. Tumour-conditioned media reproduced these distinct macrophage phenotypes in vitro, indicating that tumour-derived factors actively shape TAM identity. Pharmacological inhibition of LSD1 using baicalin or INCB059872 reduced the expression of CD206 and the immune checkpoint molecule PD-L1, consistent with macrophage reprogramming away from a tumour-promoting state. Collectively, these findings identify LSD1 as an epigenetic regulator of macrophage plasticity in CRLM, implicated in the maintenance of immunosuppressive TAM phenotypes, and potentially able to induce phenotypic reversion. Our findings identify LSD1 as a regulator of TAM phenotype and support further investigation of LSD1 targeting as a strategy to remodel the metastatic tumour microenvironment and potentially enhance anti-tumour immunity.

title: Lipid nanoparticle-mediated transcription factor EB mRNA delivery for the treatment of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease
abstract: Abstract Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is a prevalent disorder characterized by excessive hepatic lipid accumulation, frequently progressing to steatohepatitis, fibrosis, and cirrhosis. Transcription factor EB (TFEB) coordinates lysosomal biogenesis, autophagy, and lipid catabolism, and therefore represents a potential therapeutic target; however, safe and direct strategies for selectively enhancing hepatic TFEB activity remain limited. Here, liver-targeted lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) were developed to deliver mRNAs encoding wild-type TFEB or the constitutively active TFEB S211A mutant, and their efficacy was evaluated in cellular and choline-deficient, L-amino acid-defined high-fat diet (CDAHFD)-induced mouse models of MASLD. LNP-mediated delivery increased hepatic TFEB expression, enhanced autophagic flux, and reprogrammed metabolic pathways toward fatty acid oxidation (e.g., CPT1A and ACOX1 ) while suppressing the expression of lipogenic genes (e.g., FASN , ACC , and SREBP1 ). Consequently, targeted TFEB mRNA therapy significantly reduced hepatic triglyceride content, attenuated steatosis, lowered MASLD activity scores, and decreased fibrotic remodeling. Mechanistically, transcriptomic profiling, ChIP-qPCR, promoter-reporter assays, and targeted knockdown models indicated that TFEB exerts its protective effects against lipid accumulation at least partly by transcriptionally activating the fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) signaling pathway. Collectively, these findings establish LNP-mediated TFEB mRNA delivery as a useful preclinical approach for investigating hepatic biology and provide a targeted, transient, and non-integrating genetic strategy with potential for the treatment of MASLD.

title: RCCD1-JMJD5 coordinate histone demethylation to promote platinum resistance in non-small cell lung cancer via FN1-mediated epithelial–mesenchymal transition
abstract: Abstract Chemoresistance remains a major obstacle to effective treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet the epigenetic mechanisms underlying platinum resistance remain incompletely understood. Here, we show that Jumonji C domain-containing protein 5 (JMJD5) promotes platinum resistance in NSCLC cells and xenograft tumors while inducing a slow-proliferative, mesenchymal-like phenotype characterized by enhanced migration, invasion, spheroid formation, and epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT). Mechanistically, JMJD5 interacted with RCC1 domain-containing protein 1 (RCCD1), and cisplatin treatment promoted their nuclear accumulation concomitant with reduced H3K36me2 levels. RCCD1 depletion attenuated JMJD5-associated H3K36me2 demethylation and reversed EMT-associated phenotypes and cisplatin resistance, supporting RCCD1 as a functional cofactor of JMJD5-mediated chromatin remodeling. Fibronectin 1 (FN1) was further identified as a downstream effector of this pathway. Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of FN1 suppressed JMJD5-induced migration and invasion and restored cisplatin sensitivity. Notably, JMJD5-dependent FN1 protein accumulation required ongoing protein synthesis without a corresponding increase in FN1 mRNA, suggesting post-transcriptional regulation. Consistently, elevated FN1 expression was associated with unfavorable overall survival in patients with lung cancer. Collectively, these findings reveal a JMJD5–RCCD1–H3K36me2–FN1 regulatory axis linking chemotherapy-induced epigenetic remodeling to EMT-associated platinum resistance and suggest that disruption of this pathway may represent a potential strategy for overcoming chemoresistance in NSCLC.

title: Epigenetic regulatory networks in the pathogenesis and treatment of osteoporosis subtypes
abstract: Abstract Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disorder characterized by reduced bone mineral density and heightened bone fragility, encompassing primary (senile and postmenopausal) and secondary (glucocorticoid-induced and diabetic) subtypes. Maintaining skeletal health relies on the dynamic balance between osteoblast-mediated bone formation and osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. Among the multitude of factors orchestrating this bone remodeling process, epigenetics, which regulates gene expression via reversible chemical modifications without altering the primary DNA sequence, plays an essential role in maintaining bone homeostasis. While previous research has identified numerous epigenetic factors in bone metabolism, a comprehensive synthesis of their specific contributions to different osteoporosis subtypes and the corresponding therapeutic strategies remains lacking. This review outlines the major epigenetic mechanisms involved in bone metabolism, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, RNA modifications, and non-coding RNAs. Subsequently, we comprehensively elucidate how the dysregulation of these epigenetic landscapes drives the pathogenesis of distinct osteoporosis subtypes, emphasizing their roles in disrupting the osteoblast-osteoclast axis. Furthermore, we review emerging epigenetic-based therapeutics across distinct osteoporosis subtypes, ranging from systemic pharmacological inhibitors, such as DNA methyltransferase and histone demethylase inhibitors, to advanced delivery platforms targeting the skeletal microenvironment, such as engineered extracellular vesicles and functionalized nanocarriers. By integrating molecular mechanistic insights with these diverse therapeutic strategies, this review establishes a comprehensive framework for understanding the epigenetic heterogeneity in the pathogenesis and therapeutics of osteoporosis. Ultimately, it provides essential directions for future investigations, offering innovative epigenetic strategies to tackle various osteoporosis subtypes.

title: Citrullinated histone H3 and elevated polyamine metabolism gene expression in peripheral blood polymorphonuclear leukocytes as biomarkers for poor immunotherapy response in cancer patients
abstract: Abstract There is a critical need to identify validated biomarkers that can predict cancer patient outcomes. This study evaluated biomarkers of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) and polyamine gene expression in peripheral blood that may correlate with greater risk for poor response to immunotherapy. Peripheral blood collected from cancer patients being treated with chemo/immunotherapy and from healthy volunteers was analyzed for levels of citrullinated histone H3 (Cit H3, a NETosis marker), inflammatory cytokines, and circulating tissue factor positive microparticles (TF + MPs). Elevated levels of plasma TF + MPs, Cit H3, IL-8, and IL-6 each significantly correlated with poor response to immunotherapy. Since in vitro stimulation of both human and mouse neutrophils to form NETs was blocked with addition of an inhibitor of polyamine uptake (Trimer44NMe), RNA expression of polyamine/glutamine metabolism genes was evaluated in both peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMN). Elevated expression of glutamine-associated genes in PBMCs and decreased expression of polyamine-associated genes in PMN correlated with favorable patient response to immunotherapy. Although not reaching significant levels, a high overall polyamine score in peripheral PMNs as well as increased plasma Cit H3 levels correlated well with poor response to immunotherapies in cancer patients. In a mouse model of triple negative breast cancer, polyamine blocking therapy inhibited not only primary tumor growth and lung metastases but also decreased intratumor NETs. Results from this study suggest a mechanistic link between NETosis and polyamine gene expression in PMN that warrant further investigation as peripheral blood biomarkers for immunotherapy response.

title: Circadian rhythms in health and disease
abstract: Abstract Circadian rhythms, serving as a crucial temporal bridge linking neural activity and pathological biology, are regulated by central pacemaker neurons to maintain cellular homeostasis and coordinate diverse biological processes. Circadian rhythm disruption is closely associated with various diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders, metabolic disorders, and cancer. Circadian rhythms are controlled by core clock genes, such as BMAL1 and CLOCK, modulating numerous physiological processes, encompassing metabolism, immune responses, neural activity, and hormone regulation. Circadian rhythms disruptions arising from shift work, jet lag, or inconsistent sleep schedules are implicated in both the onset and progression of numerous diseases, notably Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. The article highlights how circadian dysregulation alters cellular processes to potentially accelerate disease progression. Circadian disruption results in impaired immune function, further promoting disease development and resistance to treatment. Potential therapeutic applications based on circadian biology, such as chronotherapy and personalized medicine, are also discussed. Recent technological advances, embodied in wearable devices and omics approaches, are increasingly providing deeper insights into circadian biology. Further unveiling the role of circadian in health and disease opens new avenues for tailoring treatment timing to patients' biological rhythms, thereby enhancing therapeutic outcomes across various diseases. By bridging fundamental circadian mechanisms with clinical pathology, this review provides a roadmap for future chronotherapeutic interventions in precision medicine.

title: The sirtuin family: from mechanisms to therapy
abstract: Abstract Sirtuins (SIRT1–SIRT7) are evolutionarily conserved NAD + -dependent deacylases that function as metabolic sensors, coupling cellular metabolic state to epigenetic, transcriptional and post-translational regulatory programs across distinct subcellular compartments. Despite two decades of research, isoform- and disease-specific aspects remain poorly integrated, limiting both conceptual clarity and therapeutic translation. This review synthesizes recent advances in sirtuin biology into a family-wide framework. Rather than functioning as isolated longevity factors, sirtuins operate as a distributed compartmentalized regulatory network in which nuclear SIRT1, SIRT6 and SIRT7, cytosolic SIRT2 and mitochondrial SIRT3, SIRT4 and SIRT5 collectively govern glucose and lipid metabolism, mitochondrial quality control, autophagy, inflammation and immune tolerance. This network operates across metabolic disorders, cardiovascular and neurodegenerative diseases, inflammatory conditions and cancer, where dysregulated sirtuin signalling influences disease development in a disease- and tissue-specific manner. Therapeutic strategies are evaluated, ranging from isoform-selective small-molecule modulators and NAD + -targeted interventions to emerging protein-degradation approaches, with isoform selectivity, off-target effects and the systemic consequences of NAD + modulation identified as key translational barriers that have contributed to heterogeneous clinical outcomes. Viewing sirtuins as a context-sensitive compartmentalized network, not isolated targets, offers a coherent framework to guide mechanistic interrogation and the design of more precise sirtuin-based therapies, with priority areas including tissue-selective degradation and network-level biomarkers.

title: Transcriptional and phenotypic alterations of regulatory and effector T cells in type 1 diabetes mellitus
abstract: Abstract Type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) is characterized by the destruction of pancreatic β-cells, in which the dysfunction of regulatory T cells (Tregs) contributes to impaired immune tolerance. However, Treg heterogeneity remains incompletely understood, which limits the effectiveness of current therapies. Here, we have integrated transcriptome, flow cytometry, glycemic correlation, and cross-model validation to characterize the dysregulation of Tregs and effector T cells (Teffs) in a streptozotocin (STZ)-induced T1DM mouse model. Tregs exhibited a proliferative, effector-like, unstable lineage, and metabolic reprogramming features, marked by increased Melk , Prf1 , Gzma and Hk2 , and decreased expression of Tnfsf15 , Irak3 and Zeb2 in T1DM, and alterations in the transcription-factor networks involving Nfatc2 , Elk1 , and Ahr . Flow cytometry further revealed that the frequency of splenic Tregs was significantly increased, accompanied by broad upregulation of programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1), T cell immunoreceptor with Ig and ITIM domains (TIGIT), lymphocyte-activation gene 3 (LAG3), and T-cell immunoglobulin and mucin domain-containing protein 3 (TIM3). Meanwhile, expression of glycoprotein A repetitions predominant (GARP) and latency-associated peptide (LAP) was decreased, whereas interleukin (IL)- 17 and interferon-γ (IFN-γ) secretion were increased, suggesting a Treg phenotype with high checkpoint expression and inflammatory features. Cross-model analyses identified concordant IL-15-, IL-36 A-, E2F-, and metabolic programs across the C57BL/6, non-obese diabetic (NOD), and human datasets, including shared genes Smad3 , Mki67 , and Cxcr4 . Teffs also displayed a hyperactivated but transcriptionally imbalanced phenotype in T1DM. Collectively, our findings reveal transcriptional and phenotypic alterations in Tregs and Teffs, providing new insights into T-cell dysregulation and potentially informing the development of Treg-based immunotherapies in T1DM.

title: Ferroptosis in health and disease
abstract: Abstract Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent, non-apoptotic form of regulated cell death that is driven by lipid peroxidation. In the past decade, it has emerged as a core pathogenic mechanism in a wide range of human diseases, such as neurodegenerative disorders, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and notably, reproductive dysfunction. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the molecular mechanisms underlying ferroptosis with a specific focus on the System Xc⁻–GSH–GPX4 axis, iron metabolism, lipid peroxidation, and the regulatory roles of key modulators such as Nrf2, ACSL4, and CISD2. This review also explores the physiological roles of ferroptosis in development, tissue homeostasis, and immune regulation, as well as its pathological contributions to obesity, diabetes mellitus, atherosclerosis, neurodegeneration, stroke, cancer, infectious diseases, and reproductive disorders. A substantial part of this review discusses the role of ferroptosis in the pathogenesis of reproductive disorders, such as male reproductive pathologies, including varicocele, testicular ischemia–reperfusion, cryptorchidism, oligospermia, erectile dysfunction, and testicular cancer, and female pathologies like primary ovarian insufficiency, polycystic ovary syndrome, endometriosis, ovarian cancer, and pre-eclampsia. Moreover, the interplay between ferroptosis and immune dysfunction in reproductive tract infections was highlighted. Furthermore, we evaluated current biomarkers, emerging therapeutic strategies, and key translational challenges, highlighting the promise of ferroptosis-modulating agents for novel diagnostic and therapeutic interventions in reproductive medicine and beyond.

title: EZH2 coordinates inflammatory and pain-associated pathways across joint compartments in osteoarthritis
abstract: Abstract Enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2), a histone methyltransferase responsible for H3K27 trimethylation, has emerged as a potential therapeutic target in osteoarthritis (OA). However, its contribution to the multicellular mechanisms driving joint degeneration and pain remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the effects of pharmacological EZH2 inhibition in a pain-relevant murine OA model and explored its cellular and molecular consequences across OA-associated cell populations. OA was induced in mice by intra-articular monosodium iodoacetate (MIA) injection followed by local administration of the EZH2 inhibitor EPZ-6438. Joint pathology and pain-related behaviors were assessed by histological and functional analyses. Mechanistic studies were performed in primary human OA fibroblast-like synoviocytes and bone marrow-derived cells using targeted gene expression analyses, proteomics and ChIP-seq approaches. EZH2 inhibition reduced cartilage damage, synovial inflammation and pain-related behavioral alterations in vivo. In OA synoviocytes, EPZ-6438 decreased the expression of inflammatory, catabolic and pain-associated mediators while promoting autophagy-related responses. Proteomic and ChIP-seq analyses revealed EZH2-dependent regulation of inflammatory pathways, cellular homeostasis and neuronal-associated processes, including axon guidance-related pathways. ChIP-seq further identified inflammation-dependent EZH2 recruitment to promoters of neurodevelopmental regulators, including PAX6, suggesting a potential contribution of EZH2 to neuronal-associated mechanisms in OA. In addition, EZH2 inhibition reduced macrophage inflammatory activation and osteoclast differentiation. Together, these findings identify EZH2 as a candidate epigenetic regulator linking inflammatory, neuroimmune and osteoimmune pathways across the osteoarthritic joint. Targeting EZH2 may represent a therapeutic strategy to simultaneously modulate joint inflammation, remodeling and pain-associated pathways.

title: Aquaporin water channels: distribution, physiology, pathophysiology, and relevance as therapeutic targets
abstract: Abstract Aquaporins (AQPs) represent a class of integral membrane proteins that function as selective water channels, facilitating the transit of water molecules across biological membranes. Under specific conditions, these proteins may also mediate the permeation of small solutes, including glycerol, hydrogen peroxide, urea, carbon dioxide, and ammonia. Investigations into AQPs have unveiled distinctive structural attributes and functional properties. Evidence indicates that AQPs are broadly distributed across diverse tissues and organ systems in humans, contributing to essential physiological processes. An expanding body of literature highlights the involvement of AQPs in disease pathogenesis and progression, particularly in cellular behaviors such as proliferation and motility, pulmonary gas exchange, and the modulation of non-canonical signaling pathways. This review comprehensively outlines the tissue-specific and subcellular distribution profiles, physiological roles, and regulatory mechanisms associated with AQPs. It further characterizes the alterations in AQP functionality under pathological states, delineates their involvement and mechanistic contributions to multisystem disorders, and provides an overview of therapeutic strategies targeting AQPs, along with their translational prospects. In addition, key gaps in current knowledge are identified, and pivotal research directions, such as tissue-specific modulation and the design of targeted inhibitors and activators, are proposed to advance the translational application of AQPs as diagnostic and therapeutic targets.

title: Chemical genetic screens combine target dependence with efficacy: discovery of a MAP3K1 degrader (HBC-8) with anticancer activities
abstract: Abstract Heterobifunctional compounds (HBCs) that facilitate target protein degradation (TPD) by recruiting an E3 ligase complex have emerged as therapeutic options for cancer. Current screening approaches often prioritize protein degradation over anticancer activity, potentially missing therapeutically relevant compounds. To address this, we developed a viability-based screening strategy using isogenic wild-type, MAP3K1 -knockout, and CRBN -knockout cell lines to identify HBCs with target- and E3-ligase-dependent anticancer effects. This approach identified HBC-8, which is > 30-fold more potent than the parent MAP3K1 inhibitor and induces S-phase arrest, growth inhibition, and apoptosis in a MAP3K1- and CRBN-dependent manner. HBC-8 degrades MAP3K1; however, proteome-wide, genome-wide, and large-scale viability-based screens indicate that the anticancer activity of HBC-8 also relies on the disruption of the ubiquitin–proteasome system and protein translation machinery, extending beyond MAP3K1 degradation alone. Target dependence of HBC-8 was established using a large-scale viability screen in 869 cancer cell lines, and the anticancer effects correlated with the expression levels of the target (MAP3K1) and E3 ligase (CRBN). Furthermore, HBC-8 showed antitumor effects in an in vivo orthotopic ovarian cancer model without observable toxicity, supporting the use of isogenic cell lines for chemical genetic screens as a rapid, holistic approach to identify therapeutically relevant HBCs that also degrade the target protein.

title: Effects of SGLT2 inhibition on cardiac remodeling and heart failure development in aortic stenosis rats
abstract: Abstract Aortic stenosis (AS) is increasingly prevalent in ageing populations, yet no pharmacological therapy has been shown to modify its progression to heart failure (HF). Sodium glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors improve outcomes in HF, but their effects in pressure overload-induced cardiac remodeling remain unclear. Here, we show that rats with long-term AS develop HF features, left ventricular dilation, and systolic and diastolic dysfunction, accompanied by increased oxidative stress, impaired antioxidant defenses, myocardial fibrosis, and transcriptional remodeling. Empagliflozin (10 mg/kg/day for 8 weeks) attenuated cardiac dysfunction and reduced HF features. At molecular level, empagliflozin prevented increase in lipid peroxidation, and decreased interstitial collagen deposition, while increasing glutathione peroxidase and matrix metalloproteinase-2 activity. Transcriptomic analysis identified 1,078 differentially expressed genes and revealed enrichment of pathways associated with extracellular matrix organization and signal transduction in AS. Empagliflozin predominantly regulated genes involved in cardiac contraction, mitochondrial membrane organization, apoptosis, and cell survival. Profibrotic and remodeling-associated genes were upregulated in AS, while empagliflozin induced a distinct transcriptional program associated with improved myocardial homeostasis. AS was associated with reduced activity of energy metabolism enzymes, which was not restored by empagliflozin. Collectively, these findings identify oxidative stress, extracellular matrix remodeling, and transcriptional reprogramming as mechanisms underlying cardiac dysfunction in AS. Empagliflozin mitigates cardiac remodeling and HF progression and modulates fibrosis and gene networks regulating cardiac function. These data highlight SGLT2 inhibition as a potential therapeutic strategy in pressure overload-induced heart failure.

title: Bone morphogenetic protein 12: a novel target for cardiovascular disease
abstract: Abstract Bone morphogenetic protein 12 (BMP12) is known to regulate mesenchymal differentiation and extracellular matrix remodeling. Given its structural and signaling similarities to BMP2, which promotes osteogenic phenotypic switching and pro-atherogenic responses in vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), BMP12 may also contribute to vascular remodeling and atherosclerosis progression. This translational study aimed to unravel BMP12 involvement in cardiovascular disease (CVD). BMP12 effects on atherogenesis-related processes in VSMCs in absence or presence of BMP type I receptor inhibitors (DMH2 and LDN-193189) were evaluated. Additionally, circulating BMP12 levels were measured in a well-characterized cohort of patients with CV risk factors and correlated with cardiometabolic disorders and vascular damage markers. Results from the experimental study showed increased migration and calcification in BMP12-treated VSMCs. Mechanistically, BMP12 induced expression of osteogenic markers (RUNX2 and ALP) and genes related to cellular migration ( Mmp9 ), while reducing contractile marker Desmin . These pro-atherogenic effects were blocked using BMP type I receptor inhibitors. Furthermore, the clinical study revealed higher serum BMP12 levels in patients with CVD and type 2 diabetes. Moreover, circulating BMP12 concentrations were elevated in patients with carotid and femoral plaques, correlating with plaque volume. Notably, BMP12 emerged as an independent predictor of femoral atherosclerosis. Collectively, these findings identify BMP12 as a previously unrecognized mediator of vascular remodeling, promoting pro-atherogenic effects in VSMCs through canonical BMP signaling. The association between elevated circulating BMP12 levels and subclinical vascular damage further supports its potential value as a contributor to atherosclerosis progression and as a promising novel candidate biomarker for CV risk.

title: Biological functions and emerging interplay of FGF21 and GDF15 in metabolic diseases and aging
abstract: Abstract Metabolic diseases and age-related disorders represent a major global health burden driven by the increasing prevalence of obesity and obesity-associated complications. These disorders are characterized by chronic disturbances in energy homeostasis. A key feature linking metabolic disease and aging is the activation of stress-related pathways, which contribute to progressive metabolic dysfunction. Among the endocrine mediators of cellular stress, fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21) and growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) have emerged as key regulators of metabolic homeostasis. Both are induced by similar stress conditions, including nutrient imbalance, inflammation, oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, and are elevated in pathophysiological conditions such as obesity, type 2 diabetes (T2D), metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and aging. FGF21 and GDF15 also share overlapping regulatory pathways and complementary functions, suggesting a potential coordinated regulation and functional interplay. However, the extent and physiological relevance of this possible interrelationship remain incompletely understood. This review summarizes current knowledge on the regulation, tissue sources, and signaling mechanisms of FGF21 and GDF15 across metabolic diseases and aging, with particular attention to their roles as mediators of adaptive metabolic responses and their overlapping biological actions. We further discuss their context-dependent effects under acute and chronic stress and their relevance as biomarkers of metabolic dysfunction and disease progression. Collectively, this work highlights FGF21 and GDF15 as integrated stress signals linking cellular stress to systemic metabolic adaptation, providing a conceptual framework for understanding their cooperative roles and regulation in metabolic and age-related diseases, which may have therapeutic potential.

title: Cat eye syndrome chromosome region, candidate 1 is a novel prognostic biomarker in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
abstract: Abstract Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) exhibits great prognostic heterogeneity, necessitating the identification of high-risk patients for timely treatment. This study aimed to find novel prognostic biomarkers directly from diseased cardiac tissue to improve risk stratification of HCM. We utilized a myocardial transcriptome discovery cohort ( n = 246; median follow-up 6.8 years) alongside two independent plasma validation cohorts (Beijing, n = 1,238; follow-up 2.5 years; Xi’an, n = 402; follow-up 4.8 years). The primary and secondary endpoints were cardiovascular death and sudden cardiac death (SCD), respectively. In the discovery cohort, myocardial expression of CECR1 (cat eye syndrome chromosome region, candidate 1, also known as ADA2 , Adenosine Deaminase 2) demonstrated the strongest association with cardiovascular death ( P = 9.6 × 10 –5 ). Plasma CECR1 levels correlated modestly but significantly with myocardial expression. In the Beijing validation cohort, decreased plasma CECR1 predicted increased risks of cardiovascular death (adjusted hazard ratio (HR) 3.731, P < 0.001) and SCD (adjusted HR 7.398, P < 0.001), with areas under the curves (AUCs) of 0.720 and 0.798, respectively. These findings were replicated in the Xi’an validation cohort. Integrating plasma CECR1 into the HCM Risk-SCD model significantly enhanced its predictive performance, increasing the AUC from 0.723 to 0.845 ( P = 0.031) in the Beijing validation cohort and consistently improving it from 0.600 to 0.781 ( P = 0.018) in the Xi’an validation cohort. In conclusion, CECR1 represents a novel prognostic biomarker of HCM. Measurement of CECR1 may improve risk stratification by facilitating the identification of individuals at higher risk of cardiovascular mortality. CECR1 assessment may provide additional information for SCD risk evaluation and support clinical decision-making regarding implantable cardioverter-defibrillator therapy.

title: Syncytiotrophoblast differentiation defects drive ER stress and reprogram placental PSG1 glycosylation in preeclampsia
abstract: Abstract During pregnancy, placenta-derived proteins such as pregnancy-specific glycoprotein 1 (PSG1) enter the maternal circulation, providing a window into placental health and enabling liquid biopsy strategies for monitoring pregnancy disorders. PSG1, a highly glycosylated protein secreted by syncytiotrophoblast (STB) cells, reflects trophoblast differentiation status. Circulating PSG1 levels are reduced in early-onset preeclampsia (PE), but how PSG1 glycosylation is altered in this condition remains unclear. Here, we show by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry that native PSG1 purified from healthy and early-onset PE pregnancies carries an O -linked glycan in its N domain in addition to diverse N -linked glycans. In PE, PSG1 N -glycans displayed a shift toward increased oligomannose structures and reduced sialylation. Induction of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress in primary STBs altered the glycosylation enzyme machinery, and single-nucleus transcriptomic data indicated a reduced contribution of mature STB populations in PE, consistent with an immature STB-like glycoprotein signature. Altered N -glycosylation increased binding to mannose and asialoglycoprotein receptors and cellular uptake, suggesting enhanced hepatic clearance as a possible explanation for reduced circulating PSG1 levels in PE. Our data link ER stress during STB differentiation to altered glycoprotein maturation and identify PSG1 glycosylation as a readout of a stress-impaired STB in PE. Glycan features of circulating placental proteins could therefore provide information beyond protein levels alone and complement liquid biopsy approaches.

title: Non-thermal argon plasma therapy alleviates atopic dermatitis by reducing keratinocyte oxidative stress
abstract: Abstract Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a prevalent inflammatory skin disorder associated with a considerable disease burden. Despite the advent of biologics a substantial unmet need remains for effective treatment. We aimed to evaluate the effects of non-thermal argon plasma (NAP) in patients with mild-to-moderate AD. The Eczema Area Severity Index (EASI), Numeric Rating Scale (NRS), and Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI) were evaluated following AD treatment. 16 S rRNA sequencing was used to assess alterations in the skin microbiome. A mouse model of house dust mite (HDM)-induced AD was used to evaluate the effects of NAP on AD-like lesions, immune cell recruitment, and cytokine expression. Oxidative stress parameters and related molecular markers were analyzed after NAP treatment. NAP treatment led to a significant reduction in EASI, NRS, and DLQI scores compared with the sham group, reflecting an alleviation of AD symptoms and an enhancement in the quality of life. Microbiome analysis revealed significant alterations in the microbial diversity after NAP treatment. NAP ameliorated HDM-induced AD in mice, showing a decrease in epidermal thickness, immune cell recruitment, and the expression of key cytokines, particularly interleukin (IL)− 33, in keratinocytes. Furthermore, NAP treatment downregulated oxidative stress markers, corroborating the reduced IL-33 expression and underscoring the role of oxidative stress in AD pathology. Our study suggests the therapeutic potential of nonthermal plasma in the management of mild-to-moderate AD. Further extensive clinical trials are warranted to validate these findings and understand their long-term effects and implications. Trial registration : CRIS, KCT0008949, retrospectively registered on October 10, 2023, at https://cris.nih.go.kr/cris/search/detailSearch.do?seq=25713 .

title: Super-enhancers: regulatory mechanisms, biological functions, diseases, and therapeutic targets
abstract: Abstract Super-enhancers (SEs) are operationally defined as clusters of cis-regulatory elements associated with high transcriptional activity and cell-identity genes. They display dense transcription factor and coactivator occupancy, strong H3K27 acetylation, and enhancer–promoter communication, but their annotation varies across platforms, algorithms, and thresholds. This review examines SE architecture, identification, and validation, distinguishing chromatin-based annotation from functional dependence demonstrated by locus-specific perturbations. Mechanisms of SE-associated transcription include pioneer factors, chromatin remodelers, three-dimensional genome organization, transcriptional condensates, non-coding RNAs, and extrachromosomal DNA. Physiological functions in development, immunity, and metabolic homeostasis are considered alongside context-dependent dysregulation in cancer, inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, neurological disorders, and metabolic diseases. Breast cancer provides a model for examining subtype-specific regulation and transcriptional plasticity. Particular attention is given to enhancer remodeling during endocrine therapy, cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6) inhibition, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-targeted treatment, and chemotherapy, which may support bypass signaling, stemness, and persistent resistance. Causal regulatory changes must nevertheless be distinguished from correlates of treatment selection. Therapeutic approaches targeting bromodomain and extraterminal domain (BET) proteins, CDK7/9, chromatin regulators, enhancer RNAs, and regulatory loci are critically evaluated. Definitional uncertainty, model dependence, limited reproducibility, systemic toxicity, and insufficient clinical validation remain major barriers. Priorities include standardized annotation, temporally resolved perturbation, single-cell and spatial profiling, artificial intelligence-assisted integration, patient-derived models, and biomarker-guided therapeutic development. Together, these perspectives position SEs as a context-dependent framework linking regulatory architecture to disease progression and treatment resistance, while emphasizing the evidence required to establish therapeutic vulnerabilities.

title: Circulating tRNA-derived fragments in women with endometriosis: a pilot study
